# Sotāpatti Saṁyutta (SN 55)

**ID:** SN 55
**Section:** Saṁyuttanikāya (sn)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Sotāpatti Saṁyutta* (SN 55 / PTS S V 343–413) is the eleventh chapter of the *Mahāvagga*, the fifth major division of the *Saṁyuttanikāya* [Bodhi 2003; Gethin 2001; Hazra 1994]. It focuses centrally on stream-entry (*sotāpatti*), leading modern scholarship to note that it might more accurately be titled *Sotāpattiyaṅgasaṁyutta*, as its discourses repeatedly expound the specific factors (*sotāpattiyaṅga*) associated with becoming or being a stream-enterer [Bodhi 2003; Wen, Study of Sukkhavipassaka]. In these teachings, the "stream" (*sota*) is explicitly identified as the Noble Eightfold Path [Bodhi 2003; Gethin 2001].

The collection addresses two primary fourfold sets: the four qualities defining an established stream-enterer—namely, verified, unwavering confidence (*aveccappasāda*) in the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, along with virtues dear to the noble ones (*ariyakanta-sīla*)—and the four factors that actively lead to stream-entry: associating with superior persons (*sappurisasaṁseva*), hearing the true teaching (*saddhammassavana*), careful reflection (*yonisomanasikāra*), and practice in accordance with the Dhamma (*dhammānudhammappaṭipatti*) [Bodhi 2003; Wen, Study of Sukkhavipassaka]. Many discourses are delivered to lay followers, relating stream-entry factors to lay life, severe illness, and death [Gethin 2001]. Prominent examples include instructions given to the lay disciple Dīghāvu (SN 55.3) and sickbed visitations by Sāriputta and Ānanda to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika (SN 55.26, SN 55.27), where the recollection of the factors of stream-entry serves to dispel fear and console the dying or afflicted [Nyanaponika et al. 2003; Anālayo 2016].

DharmaNexus automatically confirms extensive shared passages with Chinese *Saṁyuktāgama* fascicles (T 99 fascicles 30, 33, 36, 41; T 100 fascicles 8, 13) and aligns sections with Tibetan translations of the Mūlasarvāstivāda *Vinayakṣudrakavastu* and *Vinayavastu*, as well as Śamathadeva’s *Abhidharmakośaṭīkopayikā* [DharmaNexus]. Internally within the Pali canon, substantial text reuse occurs across the *Aṅguttaranikāya* (AN 4, AN 5, AN 8, AN 10), other *Saṁyuttanikāya* chapters (SN 40, SN 12), and the *Mahāparinibbāna Sutta* (DN 16) [DharmaNexus].
